team.name: Slavcho Ivanov
team.bio: Over 10 years of hands-on experience in catalyst changeout and reactor servicing at major European refineries including Shell, ExxonMobil, BP, Neste, ORLEN and Lavera. Has led reactor crews on site as supervisor and shift lead: planning the sequence, manning and equipment, coordinating with unit owners and turnaround managers, and running the shift on the vessel. Hands-on across the full catalyst handling chain — inert entry and life support systems, breathing air and rescue, vacuum units, screening plant, sock and dense loading, vessel internals and box-up. SCC/VCA certified (TÜV Rheinland), BA/N2 inert entry qualified, with certifications in confined space operations, crane operation, rigging and forklift handling. Deployed across Norway, Ireland, the United Kingdom, France, the Netherlands, Germany, Lithuania, Finland, Austria and Romania.

oversight.subtitle: Independent owner's site representation for reactors, catalyst vessels, columns and reformers — from shutdown to start-up.
oversight.intro: We put experienced reactor technicians on your site as your own representatives, for the whole duration of the reactor work. They watch how the work is actually done, by every contractor working on those vessels, and they tell you what they see. Every day, in writing.
oversight.quote: The licensor tells you whether the catalyst was loaded correctly. We tell you whether the contractors are working the way they should — from day one, including the unloading.
oversight.quote_note: Catalyst loading inspection starts when the reactor is already empty and ends when it is full. Our people are there before that, and stay after.
oversight.why_p1: A turnaround brings four or five contractors onto the same vessel at the same time — catalyst handling crews, mechanical fitters, riggers, scaffolders. Each of them knows its own trade. Nobody is watching how they work together.
oversight.why_p2: The plant's own people cannot fill that gap, and it is not their job to. A unit engineer knows the process. He does not know what a properly manned catalyst crew looks like, how long a reactor should take to empty, whether a rigging plan is sound, or whether a delay is genuine. The only people who know that are the contractors themselves — and they are reporting on their own performance.
oversight.time_intro: We have spent years inside this industry, on the contractor's side of it. We know how a turnaround is really run — and we know the shortcuts and the open doors that are used to stretch a job out. Some of what our people look for:
time_items: Crews arriving under-manned, with the shortfall quietly absorbed into the schedule
Equipment on site but undersized for the bed — vacuum capacity, filtration, screening
Shifts that start late and finish early, with the paperwork saying otherwise
Delay recorded as waiting for the plant when the plant was ready
Work sequenced so that standby time is created, and charged
Permits, isolations and entries not prepared the evening before, so the first hours are lost
Steps skipped in screening or loading that save an hour today and cost days at start-up
Small scope changes groomed into change orders
Inert entry and life support shortcuts — unsafe, and a guaranteed stoppage the moment somebody notices
oversight.time_note: Most contractors do good work most of the time. But when this does happen, it is invisible from the office — and it is obvious within minutes to someone who has stood in that same place doing that same job.
oversight.scope_intro: Our oversight is limited to catalyst-bearing and pressure vessel equipment:
scope_in: Catalyst vessels, guard beds, adsorber and dryer vessels
Columns — internals, trays, packing, screens, distributors
Converters, hydrotreaters, hydrocrackers, ammonia and methanol converters
scope_out: Piping, spooling, valves and lines away from the vessels
Insulation, painting and blasting outside the vessels
oversight.scope_note: If it is not a reactor or a catalyst vessel, it is not ours. This limit is deliberate and we hold it. Our value is that we know one family of equipment extremely well — not that we cover the whole plant.
oversight.contractors_intro: Scope is defined by the equipment, not by the trade. Every contractor is within our oversight while, and only while, it is working on a vessel in scope:
contractors: Catalyst handling companies — unloading, screening, inert entry, loading
Mechanical fitters — vessel internals, trays, screens, distributors, manway work
Crane and rigging crews — lifts to and from the vessel
Scaffolders — access on and inside the vessel
Specialist services on the vessel — inerting, life support, vacuum, dense loading
oversight.contractors_note: The moment the same crew moves off the reactor onto an exchanger, a line or a foundation, they are out of our scope and we say nothing about that work.
oversight.phases_intro: The full sequence, not a single work package.

phases.watch: Permits, blinding, nitrogen purge, entry preparation
Scaffold and access ready when the trade needs it, not after
Manning, equipment, vacuum performance, inert entry discipline, pace
Trays, screens, distributors — sequence and handover between trades
Lift plans, load handling, coordination around the manway
Method, sequence, coordination with the licensor's representative

do: Observe and record — on the vessel, through the whole shift, not from an office
Check manning and equipment against what the contractor promised
Follow the schedule against reality, and judge whether a delay is genuine
Watch safety compliance — permits, confined space entry, life support, gas testing, PPE, lifting
Advise on method where we see a faster or cleaner way of doing the vessel work
Coordinate on the ground with your unit owners and turnaround manager
Report daily, in writing — progress, manning, delays, safety observations, photographs
Flag irregularities, including overcharging, idle crews and work claimed but not done
oversight.goals_title: What we are there to achieve

goals.title: The reactors come back on line on or before the planned date
goals.desc: Overrun is the most expensive thing that can happen to a turnaround. Every day protected on the reactor critical path pays for this service many times over.

goals.title: Every euro spent on the vessels buys work that was actually done
goals.desc: An independent daily record of manning, hours and progress is the only sound basis for approving an invoice — or for challenging one.

goals.title: Safety on the vessels raised to the maximum, and incidents eliminated
goals.desc: Confined space, inert atmosphere and lifting over open manways are where people get killed. This is first a duty and second an economic argument: every serious incident stops the job, and a stopped job is an overrun.

goals.title: Your units are serviced better, turnaround after turnaround
goals.desc: What we record does not walk off site with the crews. It becomes the baseline you hold the next contractor to.

oversight.how_p: Two representatives, one on days and one on nights — round-the-clock coverage for the full reactor phase, without gaps at shift change, which is exactly when problems are handed over and lost. They report to your turnaround manager and work alongside your unit owners: a written report at the end of each shift, plus immediate escalation of anything that cannot wait.
oversight.people_p1: Every one of our technicians has spent more than ten years doing reactor work himself, including five years as full-time crews for one of the largest European catalyst handling contractors. Between them they have worked on refineries and plants operated by Shell, BP, ExxonMobil, Equinor, Neste, OMV, Irving Oil and Essar, among others.
oversight.people_p2: They have done the unloading, the inert entry, the life support, the loading and the box-up. They know how the work looks when it is done properly, and they know how it looks when corners are being cut — because they have seen both from the inside.
oversight.notdo_intro: This boundary matters, and we keep it strictly.
notdo: We do not cover equipment outside the list above. No exchangers, no piping, no civils.
We do not instruct the contractors' personnel. Their supervision remains theirs.
We do not take over any contractor's responsibility for his own work, methods or safety.
We do not replace the licensor's catalyst loading inspection. We work alongside it.
We do not sign off on work in place of the plant. We report; the plant decides.
We do not accept oversight assignments on any site where the contractor is a company we work for.

faq.q: How is this different from the licensor's catalyst inspector?
faq.a: The licensor's representative arrives when the reactor is already empty and is concerned with how much catalyst goes in and how it is distributed. We are there from the first day, including the unloading, and we are concerned with how the contractors work: manning, equipment, method, pace, discipline and safety. The two roles do not overlap and we work alongside the licensor, never in place of him.

faq.q: Do you cover the whole turnaround?
faq.a: No. We cover reactors, catalyst vessels, columns and reformers, and nothing else. Heat exchangers, piping, tankage, rotating equipment and civil works are outside our scope. The limit is deliberate — we know one family of equipment extremely well rather than covering the whole plant.

faq.q: Do your representatives instruct our contractors?
faq.a: No. We observe, advise and report. The contractors' own supervision remains theirs, and their responsibility for their work, methods and safety is not transferred to us. Anything unsafe is raised immediately on the spot; everything else goes into the daily written report, and the plant decides.

faq.q: You also supply crews to contractors. How are you independent?
faq.a: We never do both on the same site. We do not accept an oversight assignment where the contractor being overseen is a company we work for, and where there is any overlap we say so before we quote.

faq.q: How many people do you provide, and for how long?
faq.a: Two representatives as standard — one on days, one on nights — for the full duration of the reactor work, from shutdown to start-up. Round-the-clock coverage matters because shift change is exactly when problems are handed over and lost.
